classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the five-region dissection as two area totals, explain the identity geometrically, then independently verify it by expansion. The identity and requested proof routes are explicit, but geometric-to-symbolic coordination is required.

content.prompt: The figure opposite is made from rectangles and a square, with $AB=a$ and $BC=b$.

spec.description: Unshaded outer square with four surrounding rectangles and a central square. Top dimension arrows identify AB as a and BC as b. Ordinary source-blue outlines are rendered in house black. Coordinates describe proportions only and introduce no numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: Outer side a+b; each surrounding rectangle has dimensions a by b; central square side a-b.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source labels A, B, C, a and b are visible; inferred areas and central side lengths are not printed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain how the diagram geometrically proves that $(a-b)^2+4ab=(a+b)^2$.

answer.short: The large square has area $(a+b)^2$. Its four rectangles each have area $ab$, and its central square has area $(a-b)^2$, so $(a-b)^2+4ab=(a+b)^2$.
answer.worked:
The large square has side length $a+b$, so its area is $(a+b)^2$. Each of the four rectangles has dimensions $a$ by $b$, giving total area $4ab$. The central square has side length $a-b$, so its area is $(a-b)^2$. Adding the five regions gives the area of the large square:
$$ (a-b)^2+4ab=(a+b)^2. $$
